records.title: Flow Experience and Challenge-Skill Balance in E-Learning
records.venue: Pacific Asia Conference on Information Systems
records.abstract: Flow is an optimal experience resulting in intense engagement in the activity. People achieved flow state when they perceived balance between challenge of the activity and their skill to the activity. The concept of flow can be used to explore students’ learning performance in e-learning environment. The current research aims to empirically explore the influence of challenge-skill balance on the flow experience and the influence of flow experience on learning satisfaction and learning performance in e-learning environment. The current research conducted a quasi-experimental design with questionnaire survey and carried out an electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, a psychophysiological method. The empirical survey results have shown that challenge-skill balance is an antecedent factor affecting learners’ flow experience. Once learners reach flow experience, their learning performance and learning satisfaction would get improved. Besides, the current research also found that flow experience is relative with learners’ attention measured by EEG brainwave signal. Learners’ perception of challenge-skill balance would influence their attention in elearning activities. The current research is also in the pioneering position that using non-medical purpose EEG device in e-learning research.

records.title: Detecting Students’ Flow States and Their Construct Through Electroencephalogram: Reflective Flow Experiences, Balance of Challenge and Skill, and Sense of Control
records.abstract: Previous studies measured flow states using students’ self-reported experiences, resulting in issues regarding nonobjective and nonreal-time data. Thus, this study used an electroencephalogram (EEG) to measure the EEG-detected real-time flow states (EEG-Fs) of 30 students from the 4th and 5th grades. Their EEG measurements, self-reported reflective flow experiences (SR-Fs), grade levels (GLs), balance of challenge and skill (BCS), and sense of control, represented by their overall test performance (OA-tp) and momentary test performance (MOM-tp), were analyzed to establish their EEG-F’s construct. Based on the results of a chi-square test, the EEG-F correlates significantly with SR-F, BCS, OA-tp, and MOM-tp. A J48 decision tree analysis and logistic regression further revealed that in-flow experiences (in-EEG-F) were detected when students had high SR-Fs, where the BCS contributed to flow states. In particular, students with a low-challenge/high-skill BCS demonstrated an in-EEG-F state upon having a high OA-tp. For high-challenge/high-skill, the in-EEG-F state was determined through their MOM-tp. Through the EEG and flow state construct, this study revealed a whole-part association between students’ momentary and overall reflective flow experiences and identified viable paths for inducing students’ EEG-Fs, which can contribute to future e-learning development when integrated with a brain-computer interface for e-learning or e-evaluation systems.

records.title: Understanding Flow Experience Among College Basketball Players: The Mediating Role of Perceived Skill–Challenge Balance
records.venue: Frontiers in Humanities and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Flow experience is a critical psychological state for optimizing athletic performance, yet the mechanisms through which external situational factors facilitate this state among college basketball players remain underexplored. This study investigates the antecedents of flow experience and examines the mediating role of perceived skill–challenge balance within the framework of Flow Theory. Employing a mixed-methods design, the study collected questionnaire data from 100 college basketball players and conducted semi-structured interviews with six experienced coaches. Quantitative analyses, including reliability, correlation, and bootstrap mediation analyses using SPSS 27.0, revealed that coach leadership and support, environmental and resource support, training task design, interpersonal harmony, and team cooperation were all positively associated with flow experience (r=0.64-0.74, p<0.01). Critically, perceived skill–challenge balance significantly mediated these relationships, with indirect effects ranging from 0.0866 to 0.1020 and all 95% bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. These findings demonstrate that external situational factors enhance flow experience primarily by strengthening athletes’ perception of balance between their skills and task challenges. This study extends Flow Theory to collegiate basketball contexts and offers practical implications for coaches aiming to foster athletes’ psychological readiness through optimized training design, supportive environments, and enhanced team dynamics.

records.title: Flow, performance and moderators of challenge-skill balance
Challenge/Skill Balance, Flow, and Performance Anxiety
records.abstract: The study longitudinally tracked the relationship among challenge/skill balance, flow, and performance anxiety in 27 student musicians over the course of a semester as they worked toward a recital of a piece of music. Using hierarchical linear modeling, the balance between the challenge of a passage of music and the perceived skills necessary to play that music was found to be significantly and consistently correlated with optimal experience. Results of moderated multiple regression indicated that skill level moderated the relationship between challenge, flow, and performance anxiety. Results also indicated that flow and performance anxiety were antithetical experiences, such that when flow was highest, performance anxiety was lowest and vice versa. These findings are discussed in terms of the application of flow theory to understanding performance, and the practical implications for reducing task‐specific anxiety.

records.title: The challenge–skill balance and antecedents of flow: A meta-analytic investigation
records.abstract: Flow is an intrinsically motivating state of consciousness characterized by simultaneous perception of high challenge and skill. The position that challenge–skill balance is the primary antecedent for achieving a flow state is unclear, and more research is needed to examine its impact on flow within multiple domains. Therefore, a meta-analysis was conducted on 28 studies examining the challenge–skill balance related to flow and intrinsic motivation in a variety of contexts. The results indicated that the relationship between challenge–skill balance and flow was moderate, and smaller with intrinsic motivation. Moderator analyses revealed weaker correlations when individuals were from an individualistic culture, in work or education contexts, using experience sampling method, and self-reporting state flow vs. trait. Compared to other theorized antecedents, challenge–skill balance was a robust contributor to flow along with clear goals and sense of control.

records.title: The Effect of Perceived Challenges and Skills on the Quality of Subjective Experience
records.abstract: This article investigates the effects that perceived challenges and skills in activities have on the quality of everyday life experience. Based on flow theory it was predicted that quality of daily experience would depend on the challenge experienced and skill required in specific situations, as well as on the balance between challenge and skill. The Experience Sampling Method (ESM) was used on a sample of 208 talented adolescents to measure daily variations in four dimensions of experience (concentration, wish to do the activity, involvement, and happiness) in four contexts (in school, with relatives, with friends, and in solitude). The four dimensions of experience were regressed on the predictors challenges, skills, and their absolute difference expressing the balance/imbalance of challenges and skills. Hierarchical linear modeling, explained in detail herein, was conducted on a 1-week sample of experiences. Findings confirm the prediction of flow theory that the balance of challenges and skills has a positive and independent effect on the quality of experience. Yet some differences of parameter estimates were found between dimensions of experience and between social contexts. These heterogeneities call for a further improvement of the flow model.

records.title: Can Balance be Boring? A Critique of the “Challenges Should Match Skills” Hypotheses in Flow Theory
Enhancement of Learning Experience Using Skill-Challenge Balancing Approach
Interest as a Moderator in the Relationship Between Challenge/Skills Balance and Flow at Work: An Analysis at Within-Individual Level
From challenge-skills balance to wellbeing in sports: the role of team identification and flow
records.abstract: This study investigated the psychological mechanisms linking challenge-skills balance to psychological wellbeing among team-sport athletes, considering team identification and flow experience as the fundamental drivers of this relationship. A sample of 281 team-sport athletes completed an online survey comprising measures of challenge-skill balance, team identification, flow, and wellbeing. Results supported the hypothesized model: Athletes who perceived their competencies as congruent with competitive demands reported stronger team identification, which in turn was related to deeper flow experiences. Flow was then associated with wellbeing, mediating the effect of team identification. These findings highlight the interconnected role of cognitive resources, social identity processes, and optimal experiential states in sustaining athletes' psychological wellbeing.

records.title: The relationship between the skill-challenge balance, game expertise, flow and the urge to keep playing complex mobile games
records.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Interest surrounding the relationship between flow and problematic gameplay has surged. An important antecedent of flow in the context of video-gaming is the skill-challenge balance, but researchers have only manipulated this balance by changing speed of play. The current research seeks to examine the skill-challenge balance and flow in a mobile game in which challenge is increased via the complexity of puzzles. We predicted games like Candy-Crush would more strongly support a model of flow in which the greatest flow would be experienced by more skilled players and that high flow games would induce the most urge to continue play. METHODS: We had 60 Candy-Crush players play games near their level standing (maximal skill-challenge balance), or games that were too easy or too hard. Perceived skill, challenge, flow, and urge to continue gameplay were measured after each game. RESULTS: Players felt the highest degree of skill-challenge balance when playing games around their level standing. Easy games produced the least flow, while both regular and hard games produced comparable flow despite hard games being far more challenging and frustrating. The findings support models of flow positing those with highest perceived skill will experience greater flow. Finally, flow and arousal combine to increase urge to keep playing. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest those with high perceived skill will experience deep, immersive flow which motivates players to keep playing.

records.title: Predicting the Subjective Experience of Intrinsic Motivation: The Roles of Self-Determination, the Balance of Challenges and Skills, and Self-Realization Values
records.abstract: A series of studies was conducted to investigate the contributions of self-determination, perceived competence, and self-realization values to the subjective experience of intrinsic motivation. Using varying sets of instructions in these studies, college undergraduates generated and subsequently evaluated panels of identity-related activities. Three measures of the subjective experience of intrinsic motivation were used as outcome variables: (a) interest, (b) flow experiences, and (c) feelings of personal expressiveness. These subjective experience measures were strongly intercorrelated. Across studies, self-determination was found to be strongly associated with all of the subjective experience measures. In contrast, self-realization values made larger contributions to flow experiences and to personal expressiveness than to interest. Perceived competence, although significantly correlated with all subjective experience measures, played a considerably smaller role in the prediction of intrinsic motivation.

records.title: Flow and enjoyment beyond skill-demand balance: The role of game pacing curves and personality
Challenge in artistic flow experiences: an interdisciplinary intervention
records.abstract: This article explores the psychological phenomenon of flow through a nonrepresentational geographical emphasis on material practices. Both the positivity and skills-challenge balance assumed to characterise flow are brought into question by the challenge and negative feelings arising from material aspects of artistic practice. This challenge appears to be localised around a pivotal point in the emergence of the artwork and essential for both successful completion of the artwork and experience of flow. This localisation is conceived as a period of chimerical instability in the ontological status of the artwork, during which time the artwork is more than a series of marks but not yet a finished work, and a zone of indiscernibility concerning when activity should cease. Particular features of material practice, including heterotechnicity or cooperative framework and heterochrony or magnification of effects from small scale changes, provide a means of rethinking the skills-challenge relationship in artistic flow experiences.

records.title: Is Flow Related to Positive Feelings or Optimal Performance? Path Analysis of Challenge-Skill Balance and Feelings
records.abstract: Abstract This study examined relationships between performance, challenge-skill balance (CSB; a primary indicator of state flow) and four valence-function categories of feelings: positive-functional (PF), negative-functional (NF), positive-dysfunctional (PD), and negativedysfunctional (ND). Ten college tennis players provided 918 self-reports during competitive intra-squad matches. Participants rated their feelings, CSB, and performance during tennis matches, and the relationships between these variables were examined through correlations and path analyses. CSB correlated strongly with PF (r = .70), moderately with NF (r = .38), had no correlation with PD (r = -.03), and a small negative correlation with ND (r = -.23). CSB was more strongly correlated with functional feelings than it was to pleasant feelings. Also, CSB and performance correlated very strongly with one another (r = .81). Path analyses supported these correlations as the final model depicted strong correlations between PF, NF, and CSB, along with a path indicating that CSB leads to Performance. The results support the notion that the CSB dimension of flow is more function- and performance-oriented than it is reflective of positive and optimal experience.

records.title: A grounded theory of the flow experiences of Web users
The effects of personalized gamification on students’ flow experience, motivation, and enjoyment
records.abstract: Abstract Gamification refers to the attempt to transform different kinds of systems to be able to better invoke positive experiences such as the flow state. However, the ability of such intervention to invoke flow state is commonly believed to depend on several moderating factors including the user’s traits. Currently, there is a dearth of research on the effect of user traits on the results of gamification. Gamer types (personality traits related to gaming styles and preferences) are considered some of the most relevant factors affecting the individual’s susceptibility to gamification. Therefore, in this study we investigate how gamer types from the BrainHex taxonomy (achiever, conqueror, daredevil, mastermind, seeker, socializer and survivor) moderate the effects of personalized/non-personalized gamification on users’ flow experience (challenge-skill balance, merging of action and awareness, clear goals, feedback, concentration, control, loss of self-consciousness and autotelic experience), enjoyment, perception of gamification and motivation. We conducted a mixed factorial within-subject experiment involving 121 elementary school students comparing a personalized version against a non-personalized version of a gamified education system. There were no main effects between personalization and students’ flow experience, perception of gamification and motivation, and enjoyment. Our results also indicate patterns of characteristics that can lead students to the high flow experience (e.g., those who prefer to play multiplayer have a high flow experience in both personalized and non-personalized versions). Based on our results, we provided recommendations to advance the design of gamifed educational systems.

records.title: Flow among music teachers and their students: The crossover of peak experiences
The experience of flow and subjective well-being of music students
records.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
records.abstract: In the present study we were interested in the concept of flow – an optimal psychical state which is connected with high achievement and positive experiences. It was supposed that experiencing flow during different musical activities (e. g., rehearsals, solo performance, performance with the orchestra) should be related to subjective well being, common in life. Eighty-four students of the Academy ofMusic (28 male and 56 female) completed the Positive Affect Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS), the Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) and the Dispositional Flow Scale (DFS-2), which measures nine dimensions of flow. Results confirmed that several aspects of flow are positively related to measures of subjective well being. Clear goals, challenge-skill balance, concentration on the task, and autotelicexperience are important predictors of positive affect, explaining 36% of its variance, challenge-skill balance is an important predictor for negative affect, explaining 26% of its variance, and clear goals is an important predictor for satisfaction with life, explaining 8% of its variance. We conclude that experiencing flow is more related to emotional than cognitive aspects of subjective well being, which is not surprising, since flow is an extremely emotional experience.

records.title: Objective Difficulty-Skill Balance Impacts Perceived Balance but Not Behaviour: A Test of Flow and Self-Determination Theory Predictions
records.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
records.abstract: Flow and self-determination theory predict that game difficulty in balance with player skill maximises enjoyment and engagement, mediated by attentive absorption or competence. Yet recent evidence and methodological concerns are challenging this view, and key theoretical predictions have remained untested, importantly which objective difficulty-skill ratio is perceived as most balanced. To test these, we ran a preregistered study (n=309) using a Go-like 2-player game with an AI opponent, randomly assigning players to one of three objective difficulty-skill ratios (AI plays to win, draw, or lose) over five matches. The AI successfully manipulated objective balance, with the draw condition perceived as most balanced. However, balance did not impact play behaviour, nor did we find the predicted uniform 'inverted-U' between balance and positive play experiences. Importantly, we found both theories too underspecified to severely test. We conclude that balance and competence likely matter less for behavioural engagement than commonly held. We propose alternative factors such as player appraisals, novelty, and progress, and debate the value and challenges of theory-testing work in games HCI.

records.title: Sociological implications of the flow experience
records.abstract: The social structure of certainty and uncertainty Flow, for the most part, takes place in avocational rather than vocational activities. Although it would be ideal to enjoy one's work, and in a few fortunate societies this might indeed be the case, it is generally true in our society that most people do not find deep involvement and enjoyment in their productive work, but seek it instead in leisure activities. Csikszentmihalyi (1975b) points out that artists, scientists, surgeons, and members of a few other occupations may experience flow while working, but they constitute exceptions. Most people, most of the time, find their lives made up of predominantly nonflow situations. But what sort of experience is “nonflow”? Flow occurs in an existential middle ground. We experience it when a balance is achieved between abilities and responsibilities, when the skills we possess are roughly commensurate with the challenges we face, when our talents are neither underused nor overtaxed. Flow emerges in circumstances that are perceived as both problematic and soluble. Beyond flow are two conditions. Both represent a state of imbalance between challenge and skill. When this imbalance is brief, temporary, or task-specific, we refer to the ensuing responses as boredom or anxiety. The impact of this short-term imbalance is minimal.

records.title: Adjusting Challenge–Skill Balance to Improve Quality of Life in Older Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: OBJECTIVE: We sought to investigate whether occupational therapy that includes adjusting the challenge-skill balance improves health-related quality of life (HRQOL) for older adults in comparison with standard occupational therapy. METHOD: In this single-blind, randomized controlled trial, 56 older adults were assigned to two groups that received 10 sessions of occupational therapy with and without adjustment of challenge-skill balance. The primary outcome was change in HRQOL after 10 sessions of occupational therapy. RESULTS: Significant differences were observed in HRQOL using the EuroQol-5 Dimension score (p = .022, d = 0.76) and the eight-item Short-Form Health Survey scores for general health (p = .001, d = 0.99) and in flow experience using the Flow State Scale for Occupational Tasks (p = .008, d = 0.82). CONCLUSION: Assessment and adjustment of the challenge-skill balance of activities may effectively improve older adults' HRQOL.

records.title: Arousal of Flow Experience in a Learning Setting and Its Effects on Exam Performance and Affect
records.abstract: Abstract. Flow experience is associated with learning motivation, performance and positive affect. Therefore it is important to analyze its antecedents. An important antecedent for experiencing flow is the balance between the person's skill and how challenging the situation is ( Csikszentmihalyi, 1990 ). According to Atkinson's (1957) risk-taking model, only individuals with high hope-of-success prefer situations in which a balance of challenge and skill is given while individuals with high fear-of-failure try to avoid such situations. Integration of these two lines of research leads to the suggestion that the achievement motive might moderate the relationship between the challenge-skill balance and flow experience. This notion could be confirmed in two studies with undergraduate students (N = 57/N = 395). Additionally, flow experience was found to be a significant predictor of affect (Study 1 and 2) and exam performance (Study 2). I discuss these findings and their practical implications for academic learning settings.

records.title: Enhancing Competence and Autonomy in Computer-Based Instruction Using a Skill-Challenge Balancing Strategy
records.abstract: The present study aims to show if a skill-challenge balancing (SCB) instruction strategy can assist learners to motivationally engage in computer-based learning. Csikszentmihalyi's flow theory (self-control, curiosity, focus of attention, and intrinsic interest) was applied to an account of the optimal learning experience in SCB-based learning activities. Two empirical studies were carried out, where a group of learners were taught “Computer Networks” as part of a statutory curriculum at a tertiary institution. The empirical results suggested that a degree of self-control to compensate for the fully automatic SCB instruction strategy (i.e., competence and autonomy) would be of a greater value for learning motivation enhancement in adaptive computer-based learning systems.

records.title: Editorial: Music performance anxiety, volume II
records.abstract: Music performance anxiety (MPA) is a complex psychological and physiological phenomenon that affects musicians of all ages, genders, and experience levels, from adolescent learners to internationally renowned soloists. Traditionally, scientific literature has largely approached this phenomenon from clinical or pathological viewpoints, frequently equating it with social phobia or generalized anxiety disorder. However, the contemporary era has witnessed a profound conceptual and methodological paradigm shift. This is clearly evident in the recent collection of scientific articles published on this specialized topic.The purpose of this editorial is to synthesize these findings systematically, providing a clear conceptual roadmap for researchers, educators, and performers. This document is organized around five thematic and methodological axes, reviewing how recent studies structure the modern understanding of MPA. Together, these axes aim to depathologize performance-related stress and propose a comprehensive psychological framework that enables musicians to flourish artistically, not merely endure the stage.For decades, the relationship between physiological arousal and musical execution was assumed to follow the classic inverted-U curve (derived from the Yerkes-Dodson law), which posits that both extremely low and excessively high levels of arousal impair performance, while moderate activation remains optimal. Challenging this unidimensional perspective, Twitchell et al. (2025) reconceptualize MPA in light of advances in affective science over the past twenty years. The authors propose applying the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat, arguing that the impact of MPA is not determined by the absolute quantity of stress, but rather by the performer's cognitive appraisal. When perceived situational demands exceed available coping resources, a threat response is triggered, characterized by increased total peripheral resistance, cortisol elevation, and avoidance motivation. Conversely, when the musician appraises their resources as sufficient to meet the demands, a challenge response is elicited, leading to cardiovascular efficiency, optimal resource mobilization, and approach motivation.To measure these fluctuating states during live performance, contemporary researchers have developed and validated several context-sensitive, cross-cultural psychometric scales. Spahn and Nusseck (2026) introduce and validate the German Performance-related Questionnaire for Musicians (PQM) in a substantial sample of 605 musicians. Unlike traditional inventories that measure MPA as a stable, situation-independent trait, the PQM retrospectively evaluates three distinct temporal phases (before, during, and immediately after a concert) across three primary dimensions: symptoms of MPA, functional coping, and situational self-efficacy. The authors demonstrate that the PQM is highly sensitive to state-level fluctuations, serving as a practical diagnostic tool. The factor structure and validity of this instrument were further confirmed in a Slavic context by Kaleńska-Rodzaj et al. (2025), using a sample of 258 Polish soloists, choral singers, and orchestral musicians. Through confirmatory factor analysis, the researchers demonstrated the robustness of the three situational dimensions and their positive correlation with flow experience and generalized self-efficacy, establishing strong cross-cultural validity.In Southern Europe, Barros et al. (2024) developed and validated the Portuguese Music Performance Anxiety Scale (PoMPAS) with a sample of 414 higher education music students. Anchored in traditional tri-dimensional models (somatic, cognitive, and behavioral), the PoMPAS demonstrated excellent internal consistency and revealed a robust three-factor structure: a behavioral/emotional factor, a contextual/physiological factor, and a cognitive factor. This scale represents the first psychometric instrument developed specifically for higher music education in Portugal, integrating specific performance-related context variables such as orchestral auditions and jury evaluations.The imperative to revalidate and refine existing instruments for specific sub-populations is further exemplified by Pan et al. (2025), who re-evaluated the Kenny Music Performance Anxiety Inventory-Revised in a sample of 736 Chinese university vocal students majoring in lyric singing. Recognizing that prior validation studies failed to differentiate between vocalists and instrumentalists, they conducted exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Their results yielded a robust four-factor model: Psychological Vulnerability, Proximal Somatic and Cognitive Anxiety, Parental Support, and Memory Self-Efficacy. The authors conclude that vocalists, because they use their own bodies as instruments, experience unique physical and emotional exposure that demands a highly nuanced interpretation of the scale, especially when examined through the lens of traditional Confucian values.The experience of MPA is deeply interconnected with intrapersonal and cognitive variables that mediate or moderate well-being and performance quality. Among these constructs, musical selfefficacy plays a primary regulatory role. Ou and Qin (2025) offer a crucial contribution by differentiating between two dimensions of self-efficacy in a sample of 254 undergraduate violin students from eleven Chinese conservatories: Music Learning Self-Efficacy (MLSE) and Music Performance Self-Efficacy (MPSE). Their multiple linear regression analysis revealed a compelling, counterintuitive finding: while MPSE is negatively associated with performance-related anxiety (serving as a protective factor that promotes stable execution), MLSE displayed a significant positive association with MPA. The authors interpret this phenomenon by hypothesizing that students with high learning self-efficacy tend to impose excessively high self-expectations and rigid perfectionistic standards, thereby increasing their vulnerability to cognitive interference and sensitivity to perceived failure during public execution. Furthermore, Borges, Marinho, et al. (2026a) systematically map the relationship between flow and MPA through a scoping review of eighteen empirical studies. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, they find that while flow and anxiety are predominantly negatively correlated, they are not strictly antagonistic. Under specific cognitive appraisals, moderate physiological arousal can coexist with or even facilitate flow, provided the musician appraises the situation as a challenge rather than a threat, and maintains an optimal balance between task demands and personal skills (challenge-skill balance). The authors identify self-efficacy, emotional self-regulation, and self-esteem as key mediating variables that facilitate flow propensity and mitigate the debilitating effects of stage fright.This configuration of positive resources is explored empirically by Jiang and Tong (2024), who investigate the impact of Psychological Capital (PsyCap) in a sample of 329 Chinese conservatory students. PsyCap is a multidimensional construct comprising four positive psychological resources: self-efficacy, optimism, hope, and resilience. Using structural equation modeling, they validate a chain mediation model showing that PsyCap reduces MPA indirectly through two key mediators: self-esteem and flow experience. Specifically, students with higher PsyCap exhibit greater selfesteem, which enhances their propensity to enter flow states during performance, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in debilitating MPA symptoms. 2025) investigate a moderated mediation model of MPA among 609 Chinese music majors, examining whether perceived performance risk mediates the relationship between professional competence and MPA, and whether psychological resilience moderates this pathway. Their analysis reveals that greater technical competence is associated with lower perceived risk and lower MPA. Crucially, psychological resilience acts as a powerful moderator: the protective effect of professional competence on reducing perceived risk is significantly stronger for students with low to moderate resilience. For highly resilient students, this protective effect stabilizes, suggesting that resilience serves as an essential psychological buffer that protects performers under conditions of lower technical preparation. This resilience framework is further enriched by Du et al. (2025) in a study of 801 Chinese community choir members. They model the relationship between resilience and MPA through two mediators: performance control sense and pre-performance rumination. Structural equation modeling demonstrated that resilience is negatively associated with MPA, with performance control sense acting as the dominant mediator. Multi-group analyses revealed notable gender differences: the protective function of control beliefs is more pronounced among women, whereas preperformance rumination exerts a significantly more debilitating effect on men.The development and manifestation of MPA do not occur in an intrapersonal vacuum, but are deeply shaped by social, familial, and digital environments. Maoqing (2025) evaluates the role of perceived social support from parents, educators, and peers in a sample of 526 Chinese vocal students. Using gender-based structural equation modeling, the study confirms that perceived support reduces MPA indirectly by bolstering personal resources, such as self-efficacy, self-worth, and intrinsic motivation. Significant gender differences emerged: female students exhibited substantially stronger indirect effects, suggesting that women are highly receptive to relational support and link their self-worth more closely to socio-emotional backing.Similarly, Huawei and Jenatabadi (2024) explore social support in 483 Chinese undergraduate and postgraduate music students. Grounded in Stimulus-Organism-Response theory, they validate a model in which emotional intelligence and self-efficacy mediate the relationship between social support and MPA. The analysis highlights educational level differences: postgraduate students show stronger mediating effects, suggesting that academic maturity and performance experience enhance the capacity to internalize and utilize supportive social and emotional resources.In collective performance settings, Wu et al. ( 2026) examine gender disparities in MPA in relation to evaluative scrutiny among 774 Chinese choir singers. The authors distinguish between self-scrutiny (internal focus on rigid standards and post-performance rumination) and other-scrutiny (worry about judgment from the audience, conductor, or peers). Their structural model reveals that female singers report significantly higher MPA, and that self-scrutiny accounts for the largest proportion of the indirect pathway. They conclude that internalized evaluative cognitive styles represent the dominant mechanism explaining gender-based differences in performance-related anxiety.The rise of digital performance platforms and social media has introduced novel sources of evaluative stress. Ma et al. ( 2026) employed structural equation modeling to investigate online evaluation anxiety in a sample of 320 conservatory students engaged in digital performance. Their model demonstrates that digital performance exposure positively predicts online evaluation anxiety, which subsequently leads to higher levels of MPA than those produced in traditional contexts (on stage; not digital). This mediating pathway is moderated by two contrasting individual traits: perfectionism (which amplifies online evaluation anxiety) and self-compassion (which serves as a psychological buffer, weakening the link between evaluative stress and MPA).Contextual demands also manifest within the professional workspace. Babnik et al. ( 2025) investigated the relationship between job characteristics (demands and resources) and MPA in 94 collaborative pianists employed in Slovenian music schools. Multiple linear regression revealed that perceived job characteristics explained 50% of the variance in MPA. Perceived emotional demands (particularly, the need to suppress personal opinions and emotions to maintain interpersonal harmony) and role conflict emerged as the strongest predictors of performance anxiety. The authors conclude that collaborative pianists' MPA is not merely an individual technical issue, but a systemic symptom of organizational stress and ambiguous role boundaries relative to primary instrumental teachers.To explore how individual and environmental factors interact under different situational conditions, Bao and Yu (2025) conducted a two-study investigation. Study 1 (correlational, N = 1,364 Chinese conservatory students) showed that perfectionism and collectivist orientation significantly moderate the relationship between performance anxiety and well-being (measured via the PERMA model). Study 2 (experimental, N = 218) randomly assigned participants to individual success, collaborative success, or neutral conditions. The experiment revealed that individual success conditions-which impose rigid perfectionist standards-elicited the highest levels of anxiety. However, these individual conditions also generated higher well-being scores related to personal accomplishment. This illustrates a compelling paradox: high-pressure individual performance contexts may elevate anxiety but concurrently provide intense psychological gratification when artistic excellence is achieved. This is complemented by Takagi et al. (2026), who examined correlates of MPA in 390 Japanese professional and amateur musicians. Their multivariable model shows that attending specialized music schools (which impose early evaluative pressure) positively predicts MPA, whereas cumulative lifetime public performance count is negatively associated with anxiety, supporting behavioral habituation and extinction mechanisms.The preventive and therapeutic management of MPA has undergone significant diversification, combining traditional behavioral therapies with cutting-edge technological innovations. Bakhtiari et al. ( 2025) conducted a systematic review of coping and intervention strategies implemented between 2016 and 2023, analyzing thirteen high-quality studies (using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale). Their synthesis demonstrates that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) are highly effective in reducing cognitive symptoms and enhancing psychological flexibility. Concurrently, somatic approaches, such as yoga and meditation, significantly attenuate sympathetic nervous system arousal, validating the need for multi-faceted interventions that integrate mind and body techniques tailored to individual performers.Regarding brief, accessible interventions, Paese and Schiavio (2025) evaluated a four-week mindfulness course with twelve music students and professionals at the University of York. Practice diaries and qualitative data revealed that body-centered meditation, Vipassana (mindfulness of thoughts), and the affect-centered RAIN technique (Recognize, Allow, Investigate, Nurture) progressively fostered self-compassion and non-judgmental awareness of muscle tension. Participants reported that these practices deactivated mental rumination, restored their artistic connection to the instrument, and mitigated somatic pre-performance panic. Similarly, Bojner Horwitz and Valtasaari (2025) developed a practical, self-administered manual consisting of eighteen steps illustrated with stick figures. Tested in a qualitative case study, this manual-grounded in embodied knowledge and mindfulness-enabled musicians to observe and accept somatic symptoms without catastrophic appraisal, fostering a compassionate response to performance stress.In vocal pedagogy, Cong (2026) assesses the short-and long-term efficacy of a four-stage integrated pedagogical model termed the "Psychological Scaffolding Model" (ASSR: Awareness-Skill-Simulation-Reflection). In a mixed-methods study with a pre-test, post-test, and three-month follow-up involving 60 undergraduate vocal majors, the experimental group (ASSR) showed a significant reduction in state anxiety, improved vocal performance quality (blind expert ratings), increased psychological resilience, and enhanced heart rate variability. Qualitative analysis revealed deep transformational shifts across four dimensions: cognitive restructuring, enhanced bodily control (utilizing diaphragmatic breathing as an emotional anchor), reframing the stage experience, and developing a trusting, collaborative teacher-student alliance.Emerging technologies and simulated environments offer promising avenues for performance preparation under controlled conditions. Borges, Ribeiro, et al. records.title: Profiles of Flow Experience Among Chinese College Basketball Players: A Latent Profile Analysis
records.abstract: Background. Flow is an optimal psychological state that facilitates athletic performance and engagement. Prior research has mainly used variable-centered approaches to examine flow antecedents, leaving unclear whether athletes form distinct subgroups in flow patterns. Aim. This study identified latent flow profiles among Chinese college basketball players and examined whether these profiles differ in key situational and cognitive antecedents. Material and methods. In total, 100 college basketball players from Chongqing, Sichuan, and Beijing completed measures of flow, coach leadership and support, environmental and resource guarantee, training task design, team interaction (harmonious relationship, cooperative spirit), and skill-challenge balance. Latent profile analysis used mclust in R; t-tests and one-way ANOVAs compared profiles on flow and antecedent variables. Results. Two distinct profiles were identified: a low-flow group (n = 70, 70%) and a high-flow group (n = 30, 30%). The high-flow group scored higher on all four flow items (all p < 0.001; Cohen's d = 0.72–1.06) and reported higher coach leadership and support, skill-challenge balance, team interaction, training task design, and environmental and resource guarantee (all p < 0.001; η² = 0.30–0.59). Conclusions. College basketball players can be classified into two distinct flow profiles. Coaches should adopt differentiated interventions, particularly for low-flow athletes.

records.title: Building creative momentum: Social and psychological factors associated with flow in Chinese artists
records.abstract: Flow is a deeply immersive psychological state characterized by intense concentration, intrinsic motivation, and a perceived balance between challenge and skill. Although prior research has examined flow in contexts such as sports, education, and workplace performance, limited attention has been paid to how social, cognitive, and motivational factors are associated with flow experiences among practicing artists. This study examined the relationships among perceived social support, the positive mindset dimension, creative process, expected self/life, and flow among practicing artists in China. Drawing on a sample of 962 artists, the study employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to assess theoretically informed associations among social support from friends, family, and significant others, internal psychological factors, and flow experiences. The findings showed that creative process and expected self/life were positively associated with flow-related experiences, whereas the positive mindset dimension was not directly associated with flow. Social support was also associated with internal psychological factors relevant to creative engagement. Mediation analyses indicated that creative process and expected self/life were significant indirect pathways linking the positive mindset dimension and flow. The model demonstrated satisfactory explanatory and predictive relevance, supporting the integration of social and psychological correlates in understanding flow among artistic populations. These findings highlight the relevance of supportive social environments and internal psychological resources in relation to creative engagement and flow, while acknowledging that the cross-sectional and self-report design does not permit causal or temporal conclusions.

records.title: Off-Course: The Mystery of Teaching Higher Mathematics to Vocational Aeronautic Students.
records.venue: European Conference on Games Based Learning
records.abstract: Mathematics education remains dominated by didactic, assessment-driven pedagogies that prioritise procedural competence while often failing to cultivate applied problem-solving skills relevant to professional practice. In response to growing political and educational concern regarding mathematical readiness for life and work, this study explores the potential of immersive game-based learning (GBL) to supplement traditional approaches, shifting the emphasis from knowing mathematics to doing mathematics. Grounded in John Dewey’s (1916) pragmatic epistemology and principles of Joint Practice Development (JPD) (Fielding et al, 2005), the project investigates whether an educational role‑playing game (RPG) can support the meaningful application of higher-level mathematics in an authentic vocational context. The research focused on the design, development, and evaluation of Air Investigation: Numbers at the Scene, an RPG simulation of an aviation accident investigation. The project examined how mathematical concepts could be seamlessly embedded within a narrative to encourage inquiry and reflective problem-solving beyond rote calculation. The curriculum encompasses percentages, unit conversion, trigonometry, circular measurements, and the analysis of vector components, requiring players to employ mathematical critical thinking to solve navigational and forensic challenges. User testing was conducted with 306 post-16 learners across further and higher education. Data were collected through a questionnaire, focus groups, and interviews. Quantitative analysis revealed statistically significant relationships between in‑game progression and knowledge retention, and highlighted the influence of prior mathematics attainment on learning outcomes. Qualitative data revealed significant levels of learner engagement and narrative immersion. Most notably, participants reported a strong sense of authenticity that directly facilitated meaningful learning experiences. Key challenges that emerged were cognitive load impacting flow for some learners and interface design, particularly regarding calculator functionality. Consequently, the research highlights the need to balance narrative immersion with low-friction UI design. The findings suggest that RPG‑based learning provides a viable and engaging supplement to traditional mathematics education. By situating mathematical reasoning within purposeful, practice-oriented scenarios, this approach supports vocational learners without compromising academic rigour.

records.title: Flow Factors and Choreography Teaching Stages: A Correspondence Study
records.venue: Journal of Advanced Research in Education
records.abstract: Choreography teaching has long been organized around technique training and the production of finished works, while students’ motivational states and the quality of their experience rarely enter instructional design. Drawing on Csikszentmihalyi’s flow theory and employing literature review and case analysis, this study examines the correspondence between flow factors and the stages of choreography teaching. Flow is characterized by three preconditions (clear goals, immediate feedback, and challenge–skill balance) and six experiential characteristics. Based on the conventional organization of Chinese choreography textbooks, choreography teaching is summarized into four stages: establishing motive and theme, organizing material and training technique, rehearsal feedback and self-observation, and role immersion and stage presentation. These stages are shown to correspond respectively to four groups of flow factors: clear goals together with presentation effects, challenge–skill balance, immediate feedback, and the loss of reflective self-consciousness. A logic of “condition supply–state emergence” is proposed: teachers cannot directly manufacture flow; they can only supply, through the design of each stage, the conditions under which flow becomes possible. Three cases—Wang Mei’s modern dance drama Thunder and Rain, Matthew Bourne’s Swan Lake, and motive-development exercises in choreography classes—are used to illustrate the correspondence.

Flow Experience in the Chinese Blended Classroom: How Students and Teachers Shape English Success
records.abstract: While blended learning has become increasingly institutionalised in Chinese higher education, low academic performance in English and limited participation in English-Medium Instruction (EMI) environments remain significant concerns. Although much has been researched on technological integration and linguistic challenges, little research has examined the interaction of student- and teacher-related factors to foster a flow experience and, subsequently, improve academic performance in English. This research is based on the Flow Theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990), which examines direct and mediated relationships among student and teacher factors, flow experience, and English academic performance within a Chinese blended classroom context. The sample data were gathered from 165 non-English majors, both first- and second-year undergraduates enrolled in mandatory College English classes, using purposive sampling. A structured questionnaire comprising 38 questions was developed and administered, and the data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that student- and teacher-related factors have significant positive direct effects on English academic performance. The results of the flow experience are notably large and positive, and flow experience partially mediates the relationships between students’ and teachers’ factors and academic outcomes. The findings provide empirical support for the challenge-skill balance hypothesis of Flow Theory, demonstrating how the joint influence of the learners’ capabilities and the instructional requirements leads to optimal psychological involvement. The study contributes to existing knowledge by incorporating variables related to learners and instruction into a single structural model, which will help understand how psychological immersion can be applied to English language success within a blended higher education setting.

records.title: AI driven adaptive gamification for sustainable workforce development in corporate training
records.abstract: In today’s competitive world, gamification has been widely used to enhance engagement in corporate training. However, gamification often relies on fixed rewards and static challenges, which generate only short-term engagement and fail to sustain intrinsic motivation. This paper explores how AI-driven adaptive gamification address the limitations by personalizing learning experiences through real-time feedback and dynamic challenge adjustment. As per existing literature, this study proposes a theoretically grounded conceptual framework for AI-driven adaptivity in corporate training. It explains how AI-driven gamification enhance autonomy, competence and relatedness. It also considers how AI-driven gamification enhance autonomy, competence and relatedness. It also considers how adaptive mechanisms help optimal skill–challenge balance, drawing on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Flow Theory. The proposed framework conceptualises sustainable employee development through ongoing, adaptive, and personalized learning pathways, enabling continuous learning, long-term engagement, and adaptive skill enhancement. The proposed framework has the potential to support organisational initiatives aligned with global sustainability priorities by aligning AI-driven adaptive gamification with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, especially SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth), by promoting long- term learning and workforce resilience in corporate environments.

records.title: Examination of Dispositional Flow State and Self-Esteem of University Students Who Do Sport and Exercise
records.venue: Turkish Journal of Sport and Exercise
records.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the dispositional flow state and self-esteem of university students who exercise and participate in sports, according to gender, participation in individual or group sports, and exercise and sports participation status, and to reveal the relationship between dispositional flow state and self-esteem. The research is based on a correlational survey model. The study group consists of 400 students in total, 200 licensed athletes and 200 students who exercise, studying in various faculties of Akdeniz University during the 2017-2018 academic year. The Dispositional Flow State Scale-2 and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale were used as data collection tools in the research. Since the data showed a normal distribution, t-test and Pearson correlation coefficient test were used in the analysis of the data. A statistically significant difference was found in the transformation of time sub-dimension in favor of students participating in individual sports when students were compared according to whether they engaged in individual or team sports. In the comparison between students who engaged in exercise and those who participated in sports, statistically significant differences were found in favor of the sports group in the challenge–skill balance, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, and autotelic experience sub-dimensions. Moderate to low positive correlations were found between dispositional flow state and self-esteem in students who exercise and participate in sports. In conclusion, this study showed that students who participated in sports had higher scores only in the sub-dimensions of challenge–skill balance, clear goals, unambiguous feedback, and autotelic experience. As the dispositional flow state of university students increases, their self-esteem levels also increase.

records.title: The Science of Economic Activities — Volume 2: Principles of Economic Activities
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: The Science of Economic Activities is a six‑volume original theoretical system reconstructing the underlying operating laws of human socioeconomic development. Built upon social cooperative division of labor and labor‑time accounting, this series provides a complete framework covering research methodology, core economic‑activity principles, market mechanisms, the distribution‑and‑ exchange principles of consumer‑goods chains, universal economic constitution, quantitative formulas, core models and nine governance‑support systems. It offers theoretical references for understanding and addressing real‑world challenges including poverty, unemployment and global conflicts. As Volume Two of the six‑volume monograph series, this volume systematically unfolds the foundational principles of the discipline. Departing from assumption‑driven reasoning in conventional economics, it derives economic rules from real‑world production, division of labor, and exchange processes. It explains core principles covering consumer‑goods production, cost, net profit, currency, distribution and exchange, and clarifies the internal logic of market circulation equilibrium. Based on two unified foundational axioms and verified by the successful economic development practices of East Asian economies, this volume validates the rationality and practicality of the new economic theoretical system. The Fundamental Economic Principles to Eliminate Unemployment, Poverty and War I. Theoretical Axioms: Empirically Verifiable Underlying Premises of Economic Development (Feasibility Argumentation) Departing from the hypothesis-driven and reality-detached analytical paradigm of mainstream economics, this theory is grounded in the practical development experiences of real economies across the globe and establishes two core foundational axioms. Empirical evidence demonstrates that the total elimination of large-scale unemployment, endogenous poverty, and regional conflicts induced by economic imbalances fulfills fully objective, executable, and replicable real-world conditions for human society. From a global perspective, all essential preconditions for addressing these three pivotal global challenges have been fully established: First, the natural resources, technological advancements, and mature social systems required to eradicate unemployment and poverty already exist on a global scale. (1) The Earth’s natural resource reserves are adequate to sustain a global population of billions at the living standards characteristic of developed economies; (2) Modern technological systems capable of mass-producing abundant, low-cost consumer goods have matured and proliferated worldwide; (3) An efficient social collaborative division-of-labor system has been established. Supported by sophisticated social production models, it delivers consistent, high-efficiency output of sufficient consumer goods to maintain a modern society with universal prosperity; (4) Industrial engineering has fully standardized the production workflows, operational procedures, standard labor hours, and all technical requirements for consumer goods manufacturing, enabling rapid cross-regional replication of mature production models; (5) Collaborative production and social division-of-labor principles significantly boost aggregate social output. They enable developing economies to advance economic development through commercialized operational models and achieve cross-border replication of industrial systems alongside rapid industrialization. Second, human labor time is an inherently scarce socioeconomic resource. Unemployment constitutes a severe structural distortion of economic operations, contradicting the fundamental nature of economic systems and resulting in the waste of precious human labor resources. Case Study 1 The developmental trajectory of East Asian economies provides conclusive empirical validation of this theory. Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Hong Kong of China, and Taiwan of China have rapidly transformed from backward, poverty-stricken agricultural societies into highly developed economies with sophisticated social division of labor, successfully accomplishing social transformation toward universal prosperity and full employment. Supported by systematic, standardized economic operational mechanisms, mainland China has implemented the largest and fastest poverty alleviation and unemployment governance initiative in human history, fundamentally reversing the long-standing predicaments of widespread poverty and mass unemployment. Case Study 2 Developed economies across Europe and North America offer a second set of compelling empirical cases. These regions have largely eliminated mass unemployment and systemic poverty. The limited poverty and unemployment observed within these societies primarily stem from individual educational gaps, skill mismatches, or short-term cyclical economic fluctuations that lead to individualized rather than structural deprivation. These representative cases definitively prove that poverty, unemployment, and underdevelopment are not inherent or unavoidable destinies for any nation or region. Once an economy adopts a scientific, complete, and standardized operational system, it can rapidly escape underdevelopment and evolve from a traditional society plagued by high unemployment and widespread scarcity into a modern, developed society characterized by full employment, abundant material supply, and stable social order. This provides robust, practical evidence for the systematic global eradication of poverty, unemployment, and economically driven regional conflicts. In contrast, mainstream neoclassical economics constructs its theoretical framework on artificial hypothetical assumptions rather than authentic production and division-of-labor practices. Its analytical scope is confined to superficial market price volatility and partial equilibrium phenomena, while entirely overlooking the fundamental socioeconomic logic based on real labor input, resource constraints, and systematic social division of labor. Incapable of quantitatively explaining the structural contradictions between production, distribution, and consumption, traditional economics cannot fundamentally resolve persistent global crises, including structural unemployment, endogenous poverty, and economy-triggered regional conflicts. Conventional macroeconomic tools—including monetary policy, fiscal stimulus, and social welfare subsidies—only alleviate superficial economic symptoms in the short term and fail to eliminate recurring economic crises, structural social imbalances, and geopolitical frictions rooted in economic inequality. II. Core Ultimate Questions: Systemic Dilemmas Unsolved by Global Economics for a Century Based on the aforementioned empirical axioms and a century of turbulent global economic development, this theory refines seven foundational questions that have long perplexed mainstream economic research. These century-old structural dilemmas cannot be reasonably interpreted or thoroughly resolved by conventional economic frameworks, and they constitute the core research focus and central logical thread of this theoretical system. 1. Given that poverty eradication, full employment, and long-term economic stability are practically achievable, what are the necessary and sufficient underlying conditions to completely eliminate social unemployment, endogenous poverty, and economically induced regional conflicts? A. Principle of Full Employment: Resolve Unemployment at the Root Unemployment fundamentally originates from the structural imbalance between aggregate social labor time supply and labor time demand. The essence of full employment governance lies in achieving dynamic equilibrium between annual total labor demand and annual total labor supply across the entire society. Core Equilibrium Equation: Annual Labor Time Demand = Annual Labor Time Supply Quantitative Formula: Total Market Consumer Goods Output × Standard Labor Time per Unit Output = Economically Active Population × Annual Statutory Working Hours (Annual Total Days minus Legal Rest Days) Full employment requires not only aggregate labor time balance but also precise structural matching between industrial skill demands and worker skill endowments. Governments can popularize standardized compulsory education and professional vocational training systems to continuously upgrade public professional competencies and universal employability, enabling ordinary laborers to adapt to mainstream industrial positions. By integrating industrial engineering standards, quantitative mathematical modeling, and complete economic operational principles, societies can conduct precise numerical deduction, real-time dynamic monitoring, and scientific macro-regulation of the labor supply–demand system, thereby maintaining long-term, stable full employment. Efficient Social Collaborative Division-of-Labor System: Fundamentally Eradicate Endogenous Poverty The establishment of an efficient, orderly, and nationally adaptive social collaborative division-of-labor system is the core prerequisite for eliminating endogenous poverty. A mature division-of-labor system enables the free flow, precise allocation, and spatial agglomeration of diverse production factors, forming large-scale industrial cluster effects. This continuously reduces manufacturing costs, optimizes macroscopic supply–demand structures, balances market circulation, and generates stable, abundant, low-cost consumer goods, comprehensively elevating societal material living standards. Furthermore, a complete collaborative division-of-labor system can be complemented by inclusive social security and insurance mechanisms to address individualized poverty caused by temporary unemployment, illness, or other unforeseen contingencies among vulnerable groups. records.title: In the Zone: A Narrative Review of Flow Theory in Games, from Optimal Experience to Game Design
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: Flow---the state of complete absorption in an activity whose challenges are matched to one's skills---is psychology's account of play at its best and game design's most influential borrowed theory. This article presents a narrative review of the primary literature that carried flow from psychology into games, from Csikszentmihalyi's Beyond Boredom and Anxiety, which discovered the flow state in chess players, rock climbers, and dancers and modeled it as the balance of challenge and skill, through the Optimal Experience volume that consolidated the flow research program and Flow, the 1990 synthesis that fixed the nine components of the experience---challenge-skill balance, clear goals, immediate feedback, concentration, control, loss of self-consciousness, time transformation, autotelic quality, and the merging of action and awareness---Nakamura and Csikszentmihalyi's handbook statement of the theory's conditions and consequences, Sherry's media-enjoyment critique, Ryan, Rigby, and Przybylski's self-determination account of games' motivational pull, Sweetser and Wyeth's GameFlow model, which translated the components into game-design criteria, Chen's designer's account of adapting flow to diverse players, and the empirical studies of Engeser and Rheinberg linking flow to performance, with Salen and Zimmerman's and Juul's game-design theories framing flow among the structures of play. The synthesis is organized around three themes: the psychological core of flow, whose challenge-skill dynamics give games their experiential target; the design operationalization, in which GameFlow and related models converted the components into criteria players and reviewers can apply; and the motivational extension, in which self-determination theory and media psychology recast flow as part of games' broader pull. It is concluded that flow theory succeeded in games precisely because games are flow machines by construction---rule systems that engineer challenge, feedback, and goals---and that the theory's translation into design is a model case of psychology becoming craft.

records.title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment in a Multiplayer Learning Environment: An Exploratory Evaluation of Player Experience
records.abstract: Balancing the learning experience for players with diverse skill levels, particularly in multi-user learning environments, remains a challenge. Many game-based learning systems rely on static difficulty settings that do not adapt to individual abilities, leading to frustration or disengagement. Dynamic difficulty adjustment (DDA) aims to create a more personalized experience by dynamically adjusting the task’s difficulty to match the player’s evolving skill level, while also accommodating players with lower performance capabilities. This paper explores the potential of a DDA system in a multiplayer learning environment that includes block-based puzzles to teach programming concepts. We used a rating algorithm to evaluate the player’s performance and dynamically adjust in-game objectives. To explore the player experience, we conducted an exploratory quasi-experimental between-group study comparing the adaptive version with a fixed-difficulty implementation. The largest observed between-group difference concerned perceived competence, with higher scores in the DDA group (DDA: AVG = 2.31, SD = 0.76; Non-DDA: AVG = 1.62, SD = 1.07). However, this difference did not remain statistically significant after adjustment. No significant differences were found in perceived levels of challenge, workload, flow, or team involvement.

records.title: Expert Eyes, Machine Hands
records.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become one of the defining cultural technologies of the 2020s, transforming not only how content is produced but also how creativity itself is imagined. From text generation to image synthesis, GenAI blurs distinctions between professional and amateur practice, art and automation, originality and imitation. These shifts reach far beyond the studio or agency: they unsettle cultural hierarchies, redistribute expertise, and reconfigure what it means to author or evaluate creative work with scholars and practitioners highlighting both GenAI’s disruptive and enabling potential (Amankwah-Amoah et al.; Coffin; Hartmann et al.; Matthews et al.). As such, GenAI sits squarely at the intersection of technology and culture, making it vital to examine how creative practitioners experience and negotiate its affordances. These questions mirror broader cultural discussions about automation, expertise, aesthetics, and creativity in digital media, situating our research within contemporary debates about creativity in an algorithmic age. This article explores those negotiations through a collaborative autoethnography (Chang) in which creative professionals who are also educators worked with GenAI tools to develop an advertising campaign from concept to final artefact. By grounding our analysis in lived experience, we examine not only what GenAI can produce, but how it alters the creative process. Drawing on Csikszentmihalyi’s systems model of creativity and Bourdieu’s account of cultural capital, we situate our reflections within a wider theoretical conversation about expertise, taste, and technological mediation. These frameworks allow us to interrogate how GenAI participation affects the balance between human judgment and machine generation or between creative flow and algorithmic patterning. In doing so, we contribute to broader debates on the cultural implications of GenAI by identifying how expert practitioners sustain, redefine, and sometimes resist aesthetic standards in an era of algorithmic co-creation. The Positive Case for GenAI in Creative Practice The rapid rise of GenAI has intensified debates about its role in creative practice, particularly in creative industries where efficiency, cost-saving, and innovation are central (Cui et al.; Hartmann et al.; Matthews et al.). The issue is no longer simply whether GenAI is useful but how it reshapes the very conditions of creativity. By automating routine tasks, the technology frees practitioners to focus on more imaginative and rewarding work. As Amankwah-Amoah et al. highlight, GenAI’s transformative potential can produce “compelling” content without the burden of extensive “manual research and editing” (2), saving creative professionals time and energy that can be repurposed to more invigorating and empowering activities. Yet, as Csikszentmihalyi’s model suggests, creativity emerges from the dynamic interaction between domain (cultural knowledge), field (gatekeepers and experts), and individual (the creator). When GenAI intervenes in this system, it can rebalance these forces, enabling rapid idea generation but also introducing algorithmic biases that affect the domain of possible outcomes (Atkinson and Baker), or expectations that one can demand more for less (Matthews et al.). This theoretical perspective stresses that what feels like creative freedom can also be a reconfiguration of control. In the debates supporting GenAI, Hettrich et al. suggest that the technology can challenge human creators to think beyond the obvious by offering alternative directions that spark the creative imagination in ways they might not reach alone. Its adoption, then, is not merely a matter of convenience but a means of expanding creative possibility. What debates advocating for GenAI use emphasise is the fact that its use does not sideline the human creator. Instead, GenAI reshapes their role: Osadchaya et al. underline its function as collaborator and catalyst, enabling creatives to overcome the ‘tyranny of the blank page’, while Cui et al. highlight how it sparks novel ideas and accelerates responses to creative briefs. These perspectives make clear that GenAI should not be viewed as a competitor to human creativity but as a partner that expands its possibilities, challenging practitioners to reimagine both the process and the product of creative work. From a systems perspective, these collaborations demonstrate how GenAI alters what Csikszentmihalyi describes as a flow state: the absorption and momentum characteristic of deep creative engagement by accelerating iteration cycles and reframing what counts as exploration. Furthermore, audiences are also becoming less apprehensive about AI-generated content, with some studies showing they find AI images equally persuasive, especially in areas such as advertising and brand communication (Hartmann et al.). This suggests that combining GenAI with human expertise can enhance both the creative potential of the work and its acceptance by audiences. The Negative Case for GenAI in Creative Practice Despite GenAI’s growing value in creative processes, anxieties remain that it could displace professionals and dilute the aesthetic and quality standards traditionally associated with creative work that is exclusively human-made (Amankwah-Amoah et al.; Coffin). Scholars such as Runco contend that GenAI produces only “pseudo-creativity” (1), outputs that may appear effective but lack the contextual grounding and cultural depth of human innovation. Creative professionals echo this scepticism, observing that while AI can generate polished drafts, the raw outputs often feel “off” (Matthews et al. 15) or are “formulaic” outputs that undermine the intrinsic drive for experimentation and play that defines creative practice (Runco 1). These critiques highlight a deeper concern that, as GenAI becomes more widely adopted, the benchmarks by which creativity is judged may be lowered or distorted. Furthermore, from a Bourdieusian lens, the tension between technology and expertise reflects a struggle over cultural capital and taste: if expertise is what legitimises creativity, then the automation of creative labour threatens to redistribute symbolic power toward technological systems. The democratisation of generative tools, then, adds another layer of complexity. With platforms like DALL·E and Midjourney enabling anyone to produce seemingly professional content, the boundaries of what counts as valuable creativity risk becoming blurred (Ahmed and Ali; Chamakiotis and Panteli; Matthews et al.). Studies point to both the promise and the peril of this accessibility. Namely, GenAI lowers barriers to participation, but in doing so, it may also flood cultural spaces with superficial, poorly developed, distorted work (Ahmed and Ali), referred to openly as ‘AI slop’ (Smith and Southerton). The degradation of creative content could be inevitable because, as Chamakiotis and Panteli argue, GenAI privileges speed and quantity over originality and finesse. In professional settings, this tension becomes evident as GenAI enables less experienced practitioners to produce more polished work, but excessive dependence on the technology may hinder the growth of critical thinking and the refinement of creative skills (Hettrich et al.). Taken together, these dynamics raise important questions about how to preserve aesthetic standards and creative depth in an era where content creation is increasingly democratised. Accordingly, expertise remains crucial. Creativity has long been judged not only by novelty but also by peer recognition, audience reception, or what Csikszentmihalyi refers to as gatekeepers. Experts are well-placed to uphold aesthetic and quality standards because they understand the rules and practices that govern their discipline. As Bourdieu argued, those with cultural competence are deemed the most versed in encoding value in creative work and by extension maintain “explicit or implicit schemes of perception and appreciation” (2). Previous studies highlight this point, showing that while professionals view GenAI as helpful for generating ideas or producing early drafts, they stress that only a specialist can refine those outputs into work that is truly original and meaningful (DiStefano et al.; Matthews et al.). In this sense, the value of expertise lies not in resisting technology but in knowing how to use it effectively, drawing out its benefits while guarding against formulaic or tone-deaf outcomes, especially given the copyright infringement concerns that accompany GenAI-produced work. As scholars have contended, copyright conflict in creative industries stems from GenAI models using vast amounts of protected works as training data without permission (Lucchi; Torrance and Tomlinson). Supporters claim this ‘fair training’ is transformative, non-expressive, and socially beneficial (Lucchi; Torrance and Tomlinson), while critics see it as misappropriation that enables derivative, market-harming outputs (Lucchi; Torrance and Tomlinson). Given the loose legal restrictions that currently exist, it falls, in part, to creative experts to operate GenAI technology cautiously to prevent the misuse and exploitation of the creative work of others. Approaching the Research Our research set out to investigate how we, as experts in visual communication, experience GenAI. We are not only creative professionals with years of experience in our respective industries, but also academics responsible for teaching undergraduates the skills required for effective visual communication, positioning us as both practitioners and gatekeepers of disciplinary standards. As part of our research, we aimed to understand not only the functional opportunities and challenges presented by these technologies, but also the evaluative judgments that can be made about AI-generated content.
