records.title: Evaluating interaction mechanics in virtual reality gaming: from user studies to design recommendations
records.abstract: By utilizing six-degrees-of-freedom (6DoF) interaction, virtual reality (VR) gaming often places greater demands on both the user’s motor skills and cognitive resources compared to gaming on non-immersive platforms. Satisfying VR interaction mechanics (IMs) should facilitate a state of flow by balancing challenge and enjoyment while minimizing negative VR-induced symptoms and effects (VRISE) that threaten user comfort and overall experience. In this paper, we present the results of three user studies involving a total of 90 participants (N = 30 per study), examining how different customizable parameters of commonly encountered IMs ( slash, pick-and-place, shoot ) affect both objective performance measures and subjective measures of player experience, workload, and VRISE. The studies were conducted in a laboratory environment utilizing a specialized testing platform. Our results indicate a general agreement between subjective measures of challenge, workload, and competence and measures of task performance. Observable variations in preferences among participants suggest there may not be a one-size-fits-all approach to implementing each of the tested mechanics. While participants most commonly preferred parameter configurations they deemed comparatively less demanding, for certain parameters a level of added challenge appeared to contribute toward a more fun experience. Despite a level of physical exertion experienced during the study session, participants reported a relatively low intensity of VRISE. Based on these findings, we propose a set of IM-specific recommendations for implementing the three mechanics investigated in this study. The proposed recommendations provide practical guidance for designing configurable VR IMs that balance player experience, performance, and comfort.

records.title: Flow-Related Engagement in Children Undergoing Cancer Treatment in China: A Scoping Review of Psychosocial and Digital Interventions
records.abstract: This scoping review aims to map and synthesize existing evidence regarding flow-related engagement among children undergoing cancer treatment in China, with a particular focus on psychosocial and digital interventions. Flow theory describes an optimal psychological state characterized by deep concentration, intrinsic motivation, perceived control, enjoyment, and balance between challenge and skill. Although flow has been extensively studied in educational, occupational, and digital contexts, its application in pediatric oncology remains limited. Existing interventions used in pediatric oncology, including therapeutic play, expressive arts, medical play, shared reading, virtual reality, and digital gaming, frequently incorporate elements associated with flow-related engagement; however, these mechanisms have not been systematically mapped. This scoping review will identify and characterise psychosocial and digital interventions that promote engagement-related experiences among children undergoing cancer treatment in Chinese contexts. The review will examine how flow-related constructs are conceptualised, operationalised, and represented within existing interventions and will identify gaps requiring future research.

records.title: Redefining Digital Education: The Impact of AI-Driven Flow Experience on Learner Satisfaction and Continuous Intention
records.abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into online learning systems has significantly transformed the landscape of digital education. Grounded in a comprehensive theoretical framework, this study draws upon Flow Experience (FLE) theory, the Technology Acceptance Model's (TAM) construct of perceived usefulness (PU), and the Expectation-Confirmation Model (ECM) to examine the determinants of learners' engagement and sustained usage intentions within AI-powered learning systems. Specifically, this research investigates the influence of key FLE antecedents—confirmation (CONF), challenge-skills balance (CSB), perceived information fit-to-task (PIFT), and online learning self-efficacy (OLSE)—on the formation of FLE. Additionally, it explores the role of CONF in shaping PU and satisfaction (SAT), the impact of PU on both SAT and continuous intention (CI), and the mediating role of FLE in influencing SAT and CI. Empirical data were collected through an online survey of 307 users of an AI-assisted online learning system in Taiwan and were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that all antecedents significantly influence FLE, with CONF showing strong positive associations with PU and SAT, while FLE has a significant impact on both SAT and CI. The study's novelty lies in its theoretical integration of FLE with ECM and TAM, providing a comprehensive account of learner engagement in AI-assisted online learning contexts. These findings offer valuable insights for platform designers and educators.

records.title: The Relationship Between Flow, Task Difficulty, and Performance
records.abstract: This project pertains to secondary analyses of a lab study dataset (N = 257), containing performance data for two rounds of the online game Tetris, each played on either a balanced or on an excessive challenge level, as well as participants' self-reports of flow experiences, perceived skill-challenge balance, and performance evaluations while playing. The purpose of these secondary analyses is to examine the relationship between flow, subjective and objective performance, and task difficulty. We expect flow to be positively related to performance both on the subjective and objective level, even though the relationship on the subjective level is thought to be stronger. We further expect this relationship to remain significant when accounting for practice effects over time, task difficulty, and interindividual differences, as well as to be detectable both on the within-person and the between-person level. Moreover, we expect flow to mediate task difficulty effects on performance, and flow in the first round to show a lagged association with performance in the second round of Tetris. Together, these findings should provide insight into the role of inherently motivating experiences like flow for task performance and what performance enhancements in flow can reasonably be expected.

records.title: Understanding Flow Experience Among College Basketball Players: The Mediating Role of Perceived Skill–Challenge Balance
records.venue: Frontiers in Humanities and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Flow experience is a critical psychological state for optimizing athletic performance, yet the mechanisms through which external situational factors facilitate this state among college basketball players remain underexplored. This study investigates the antecedents of flow experience and examines the mediating role of perceived skill–challenge balance within the framework of Flow Theory. Employing a mixed-methods design, the study collected questionnaire data from 100 college basketball players and conducted semi-structured interviews with six experienced coaches. Quantitative analyses, including reliability, correlation, and bootstrap mediation analyses using SPSS 27.0, revealed that coach leadership and support, environmental and resource support, training task design, interpersonal harmony, and team cooperation were all positively associated with flow experience (r=0.64-0.74, p<0.01). Critically, perceived skill–challenge balance significantly mediated these relationships, with indirect effects ranging from 0.0866 to 0.1020 and all 95% bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. These findings demonstrate that external situational factors enhance flow experience primarily by strengthening athletes’ perception of balance between their skills and task challenges. This study extends Flow Theory to collegiate basketball contexts and offers practical implications for coaches aiming to foster athletes’ psychological readiness through optimized training design, supportive environments, and enhanced team dynamics.

records.title: The More Dazzling the Technology, the Thinner the Culture? A Flow Theory Reflection on the "Superficialization" Dilemma of AR Cultural Tourism and Industry Transformation Pathways
records.venue: Academic Journal of Management Science and Engineering
records.abstract: Driven by "technological showmanship," AR cultural tourism experiences exhibit a "superficialization" dilemma characterized by excessive sensory immersion yet insufficient cultural understanding, forming a paradox of "the more immersed in technology, the more alienated from culture." Based on the "challenge-skill balance" framework of Flow Theory and introducing Cognitive Load Theory as an analytical tool, this study diagnoses the flow disruption mechanism caused by cognitive overload and insufficient interaction depth in AR experiences. The findings reveal three interrelated problems in current AR cultural tourism projects: overdevelopment of sensory immersion, superficiality of interaction forms, and absence of meaning construction. The root causes lie in challenge-skill imbalance, alienation of immediate feedback, and the overshadowing of cultural goals by technological goals. Accordingly, this paper proposes three macro-level optimization pathways for the AR cultural tourism industry: constructing a hierarchical narrative system, establishing industry-wide cognitive load regulation standards, and advocating "blank space" design ethics, providing theoretical foundations and strategic references for the transformation of AR cultural tourism from an "attention economy" to an "experience economy."

records.title: Current Hiring Trends in the Animation & VFX Industry
records.abstract: The computer animation and VFX industry is navigating a period of sustained transition, marked by technological acceleration, shifting production models, and cyclical workforce contraction and expansion. For those responsible for building and sustaining creative teams, hiring today involves not only identifying talent, but balancing training investment, long-term growth, and uncertainty within an evolving global ecosystem. This panel foregrounds that first-person reality. Current Hiring Trends in the Animation and VFX Industry convenes recruiting leaders from across major animation, VFX, and design studios, including Framestore, Laika, The Third Floor, and more. Rather than offering a prescriptive how-to, the panel is designed as a candid, comparative conversation shaped by those actively navigating hiring decisions, internship programs, and evolving skill demands. For students, early-career artists, and technologists, hiring is often an opaque experience. For educators, the challenge lies in preparing graduates for realities that shift faster than curricula can. This panel aims to provide an accurate snapshot of the current job landscape, clarifying how internship and entry-level pipelines actually function, outlining the flow of the recruiting and application process from multiple studio perspectives, and identifying the skills and areas of focus most in demand today. Panelists will also address best practices for pursuing work in this highly competitive field, alongside opportunities for informal connection and dialogue. Moderated by an animator/educator with a broad industry background and direct engagement in student recruitment pathways, the session emphasizes shared insight over studio competition. Through aligned concerns, nuanced perspective, and respectful disagreement, the panel models how knowledge can be shared across institutional boundaries in service of a healthier, more transparent ecosystem. By equipping artists and educators with clearer information and realistic expectations, this conversation helps transform uncertainty into more targeted preparation, and supports more sustainable pathways from education into professional practice.

records.title: From Case Reports to Editorial Leadership: A Roadmap for Trainee Engagement in Academic Publishing
records.abstract: INTRODUCTION: WHY RESIDENT INVOLVEMENT MATTERS Publication represents a meaningful milestone during clinical training; one that signals scholarly engagement, intellectual growth, and entry into the academic community. Yet for many trainees, this goal can feel daunting, often perceived as reserved for a select few with prior research experience or established mentorship. Case reports, however, offer an accessible and impactful pathway for trainees at all levels to begin their publishing journey. The ACG Case Reports Journal (ACGCRJ) serves as a central platform where residents and fellows can develop foundational skills in scholarly writing, critical appraisal, and academic inquiry. Participation in case-based scholarship fosters intellectual curiosity, encourages thoughtful clinical reflection, and provides an early and tangible introduction to academic medicine during the formative years of training. Prior work has demonstrated that early exposure to scholarly activity is associated with sustained academic engagement later in one's career. Residents who produced above-average publications before residency had significantly higher publication output during both residency and fellowship (P < 0.001), and a higher number of publications during residency was independently associated with academic career placement (P = 0.002).1 Similarly, physicians who published as primary authors during training were significantly more likely to pursue academic medicine (odds ratio [OR] 1.25, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.0–1.5), and those who completed a fellowship had nearly 4 times the odds of an academic career compared with those who did not (OR 3.77, 95% CI: 2.0–7.2).2 The aim of this editorial is to demystify the case report publication process and provide a practical, trainee-focused framework for developing, writing, and submitting high-quality case reports to the ACGCRJ. By outlining common challenges and offering actionable strategies to overcome them, we seek to empower residents and fellows to engage confidently in scholarly activity, view publication as an attainable goal, and leverage case reports as a gateway to lifelong academic involvement. To provide structure for this discussion, we conceptualize trainee engagement in academic publishing along a four-stage continuum: Exposure, in which trainees encounter case-based scholarship and develop foundational writing skills through case report authorship; Participation, through active involvement in peer review and scholarly critique; Contribution, via sustained authorship, editorial roles, and academic output; and Leadership, through service on editorial boards, mentorship of junior trainees, and advocacy for an inclusive scholarly culture. This framework reflects the natural progression of academic development during residency and fellowship and serves as the organizational foundation for the guidance that follows. WRITING AND SUBMITTING CASE REPORTS: GETTING STARTED Below are the major steps for preparing and writing case report (Figure 1).Figure 1.: A stepwise approach to writing and submitting a case report.Step I: Identify a publishable case The first, and arguably most important, step in writing a case report is selecting an appropriate and compelling case.3 Successful authors should focus on cases that pique their own intellectual curiosity while also considering characteristics that have historically been associated with publishable case reports.4,5 These include: Rare diseases or uncommon clinical entities. Novel presentations or atypical manifestations of common diseases. Unique or illustrative imaging, endoscopic findings, or procedural videos. Noteworthy adverse effects or unexpected therapeutic benefits of medications. Step II: Conduct a focused literature review Once a case of interest is identified, effective preparation begins with a thorough and focused review of the existing literature. This process should be guided by a clearly defined question related to the disease itself, a distinctive feature of the case, or the specific clinical context it highlights.4,6 Authors should prioritize high-quality, peer-reviewed sources using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, or Google Scholar. Careful documentation and organization of references at this stage facilitate accurate citation and coherent synthesis during manuscript development. Step III: Define the central message and learning points Equally important is clarifying the educational message of the case report. Authors should articulate clear learning points that anchor the narrative and guide the reader. These may address disease pathophysiology, diagnostic challenges, therapeutic decision-making, management strategies, or broader lessons in clinical reasoning and judgment.7 A focused message helps distinguish high-quality case reports from purely descriptive narratives. Step IV: Craft a clear clinical narrative Beyond identifying learning points and selecting figures, authors should focus on constructing a coherent and engaging clinical narrative. A strong case report tells a focused story: presenting the clinical problem, outlining the diagnostic reasoning, highlighting key decision points, and explaining how the case adds to existing knowledge. Avoid exhaustive timelines or unnecessary laboratory data; instead, emphasize information that directly supports the central message. Clear narration helps readers follow the clinical reasoning process and enhances the educational impact of the case. Step V: Select impactful figures Figures play a critical role in enhancing the educational value of case reports. High-quality endoscopic images, radiographic studies, and histopathologic findings can substantially strengthen a submission when they directly support the teaching objectives of the case.5 Figures should be carefully selected, appropriately annotated when necessary, and accompanied by concise legends that reinforce—rather than repeat—the key learning points. Step VI: Choose the appropriate submission format In addition to traditional case reports, the ACGCRJ offers an image-based submission format that highlights unique and educational endoscopic, radiographic, or histopathologic findings with minimal accompanying narrative. The journal also accepts video-based submissions, which are particularly well suited for demonstrating dynamic endoscopic techniques, procedural nuances, and visually instructive findings. Developing skills in video editing can be an invaluable part of this process, allowing trainees to effectively present cases, enhance visual storytelling, and share educational content with the broader GI community—while also contributing to personal growth and academic skill development. This option provides an excellent entry point for trainees, particularly those early in training, to engage in scholarly activity while developing skills in visual diagnosis and concise teaching. Image submissions are especially well suited for cases in which the primary educational value lies in the visual findings rather than an extensive clinical discussion. Step VII: Prepare for submission Authors should address practical considerations early in the process, including obtaining patient consent when required, ensuring complete deidentification of clinical data and images, and reviewing journal-specific submission guidelines before writing. Developing a clear outline aligned with the journal's structure can streamline manuscript preparation and reduce unnecessary revisions. Limitations of case reports Beyond procedural preparation, aspiring authors should also approach case report writing with a clear-eyed appreciation of the format's inherent limitations. While case reports offer an accessible and impactful entry point into academic publishing, trainees and reviewers alike should remain mindful of their intrinsic constraints. As a study design, case reports occupy the lower rungs of the evidence hierarchy, providing observational snapshots that cannot establish causality or be generalized beyond the individual patient. They are therefore best understood as hypothesis-generating contributions rather than definitive evidence. In addition, the publication landscape for case reports is susceptible to novelty bias, wherein unusual or dramatic presentations are disproportionately accepted, while informative negative outcomes or common disease manifestations with atypical features may receive less attention; a dynamic that can skew the cumulative literature. Considerations concerning equity also warrant acknowledgment: access to scholarly mentorship, protected academic time, and institutional infrastructure for research varies considerably across training programs, potentially disadvantaging trainees at community or underresourced programs. Recognizing these structural barriers is essential to fostering a more inclusive and representative academic publishing culture. Awareness of these limitations does not diminish the value of case-based scholarship; rather, it reflects the critical appraisal that defines a thoughtful and responsible clinician-scholar. Common pitfalls and practical solutions Common pitfalls in case report writing include poor case selection, unfocused narratives with excessive or irrelevant detail, suboptimal image quality, and overinterpretation of findings beyond the available evidence.8 Many of these challenges can be mitigated through comprehensive literature review, early clarification of the case's educational message, and supervision from experienced authors. Familiarity with previously published articles in the ACGCRJ can further help trainees develop an understanding of effective structure, scope, and scholarly tone. BECOMING A PEER REVIEWER AS A RESIDENT Peer review is a foundational component of academic medicine and an important avenue through which residents can actively engage in scholarly discourse. For medical trainees, peer review involves evaluating submitted work, providing constructive and thoughtful feedback, and assessing whether manuscripts meet appropriate educational and scientific standards. Participation in the peer-review process offers numerous benefits during training and early academic careers, including improvement in scientific writing, enhanced critical appraisal skills, and development of effective communication and teaching abilities.9 In addition, peer review fosters professionalism, collegiality, and a sense of belonging within the academic community. For many residents, involvement in peer review and academic scholarship may initially feel intimidating. However, several accessible pathways exist for trainees interested in becoming peer reviewers. Identifying a mentor represents a critical first step. When goals and interests align, experienced mentors can provide guidance in manuscript evaluation, scientific reasoning, and ethical responsibilities inherent to peer review, while offering early exposure to the review process.10 Beyond mentorship-based opportunities, residents may also pursue direct involvement with the ACGCRJ. As a journal specifically designed for trainees, ACGCRJ actively encourages residents and fellows to participate in peer review. Interested individuals may register as reviewers through Editorial Manager, the journal's official submission and review platform, or contact the editorial office directly to express interest. This inclusive approach lowers traditional barriers to entry and allows motivated trainees to contribute meaningfully to the academic mission of the journal. What makes a great trainee reviewer Effective trainee reviewers share several key attributes that enhance both the quality of reviews and the educational experience for authors11: Constructive and respectful tone, emphasizing improvement rather than criticism. Focus on educational value, particularly clarity of learning points and clinical relevance. Attention to structure and organization, including logical flow and adherence to journal guidelines. Critical appraisal grounded in evidence, with suggestions supported by literature when appropriate. Specific and actionable feedback, avoiding vague or generic comments. Awareness of scope, recognizing when revisions are feasible vs when limitations are inherent. Commitment to timeliness, respecting authors' efforts and editorial workflows. Exceptional reviewer contributions may be formally recognized through honors such as the ACGCRJ Reviewer of the Month award, highlighting outstanding commitment to trainee-led peer review. In addition, participation in the review process fosters the development of critical appraisal and scholarly writing skills and provides valuable opportunities to connect with editorial board members, reinforcing peer review as a skill set that can be learned, refined, and applied throughout an academic career. Ethical considerations in peer review Ethical conduct is central to the integrity of the peer-review process. Trainee reviewers must maintain strict confidentiality of all submitted materials and should not share manuscripts, images, or data outside the review process. Potential conflicts of interest—including personal, professional, or institutional relationships with authors or subject matter—should be disclosed promptly to the editorial team. Reviewers should provide objective, unbiased assessments and avoid using privileged information gained through peer review for personal or academic advantage. In addition, reviewers should exercise caution in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools during peer review. Manuscripts or portions of submitted content should not be copied, uploaded, or shared with AI platforms in a manner that compromises confidentiality or intellectual property. When permitted by journal policy, AI tools may be used only in a limited and responsible manner, such as for general language refinement, without reproducing or disclosing manuscript content. EDITORIAL AND LEADERSHIP OPPORTUNITIES Trainees can gain access to a broad range of editorial and leadership opportunities at ACGCRJ. The ACGCRJ is distinctive in that it is edited exclusively by gastroenterology fellows, creating a uniquely trainee-driven and supervised environment for developing editorial judgment, advanced critical appraisal skills, and academic leadership. Service on the editorial board offers structured exposure to manuscript decision making and the inner workings of academic publishing.12 In addition to editorial board roles, the journal expanded leadership opportunities for internal medicine residents with the introduction of a dedicated Social Media Ambassador role in 2025. In this capacity, residents collaborate closely with the Editorial Board to disseminate published cases, podcasts, and “Image of the Month” features across professional social media platforms, including X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn. This role allows residents to cultivate a professional gastroenterology-focused digital presence, demonstrate early leadership and academic engagement, and gain visibility within the GI community before fellowship training. Moreover, it supports the translation of complex clinical and public health information into accessible educational content for broader audiences.13 To position oneself for success in editorial and leadership roles, several foundational principles are essential. As with any scholarly endeavor, consistent engagement and deliberate practice are key to skill development. Attention to detail, professionalism in communication, reliability, and adherence to deadlines are critical attributes of effective reviewers and editors and are often factors considered for advancement and recognition, including honors such as Reviewer of the Month. Sustained involvement with journals such as the ACGCRJ also facilitates the development of enduring professional relationships in national societies such as American College of Gastroenterology. Many trainees participate in formal mentorship structures in which they are paired with senior editors who provide longitudinal guidance on career development, advanced fellowship training, and academic opportunities that extend beyond the editorial term. In addition, service on a national trainee-led editorial board fosters a unique sense of camaraderie among motivated residents and fellows across institutions. These connections frequently evolve into long-term collaborations, with peers becoming future colleagues, coinvestigators, and trusted academic partners throughout one's career. PRACTICAL ADVICE FOR BALANCING RESIDENCY AND SCHOLARSHIP During residency, trainees must continuously balance the demands of patient care with research and other scholarly activities. Limited time and competing clinical responsibilities are among the most frequently cited barriers to sustained academic engagement.14,15 Survey data confirm the breadth of these barriers: in a study of 57 medical trainees, time constraints, insufficient statistical and methodology training, competing educational commitments, and inadequate incentives were the most commonly cited obstacles to research participation.15 Yet despite these challenges, most respondents expressed genuine interest in engaging in scholarly activity, with increased funding and institutional incentives identified as the most impactful facilitators. These perceived obstacles can discourage otherwise motivated trainees from pursuing scholarly work. Residents who successfully participate in scholarly work despite these constraints often view academic activity not as an added burden, but as an integrated and purposeful component of their clinical training. At the individual level, residents who engage consistently in scholarship can achieve meaningful output, with a qualitative study showing that 93% produced peer-reviewed publications and many presented at regional (79%) and national (64%) levels.16 Strategic time management plays a central role in maintaining this balance. Coordinating scholarly efforts over time and setting aside brief, regular blocks dedicated to writing or manuscript review have been associated with increased and more sustained research productivity among residents.17 Establishing realistic and clearly defined goals further supports this approach. Rather than pursuing multiple projects simultaneously, residents often achieve greater success by focusing on a single, well-scoped scholarly task, which promotes follow-through and reduces cognitive overload. This strategy aligns with cognitive load theory, which demonstrates that excessive simultaneous demands impair learning and task performance.18 Importantly, many scholarly contributions arise directly from routine patient care. Clinical encounters characterized by diagnostic uncertainty, atypical presentations, or unexpected outcomes frequently serve as the foundation for case reports and other academic work. With early mentorship and timely, organized documentation, these observations can be efficiently transformed into meaningful and publishable scholarship.16 CONCLUSION As outlined through the 4-stage continuum of exposure, participation, contribution, and leadership, residents at every stage of training have meaningful opportunities to engage in scholarly activity. Scholarly engagement may begin early in residency through case report authorship, evolve into participation in peer review, and ultimately extend to editorial and leadership roles that foster professional growth and academic development. Approaching scholarship through small, clearly defined projects and viewing journal involvement as a longitudinal learning process allows residents to build confidence, practical skills, and a scholarly identity while maintaining the demands of clinical training. As a resident-driven and fellow-driven journal, the ACGCRJ provides an accessible and supportive entry point into academic publishing, empowering trainees to develop essential academic skills while opening pathways toward fellowship training and long-term engagement in academic medicine. records.abstract: Despite the transformative potential of art therapy in enhancing psychological resilience, geographical barriers and traditional structural constraints continuously hinder adults' access to face-to-face interventions. This study adopts an innovative approach to investigate the effectiveness of "Online Intuitive Painting" in facilitating flow experiences and reducing perceived stress within a transnational context encompassing Iran and Turkey. Utilizing an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, an 8-week intervention was first implemented in synchronous online creative environments (SOCE). Quantitative data were gathered via the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) and the Flow State Scale (FSS), followed by in-depth semi-structured interviews to unveil the subjective layers of these lived experiences. Quantitative findings (N=60) demonstrated a statistically significant increase in flow indicators and a tangible reduction in post-intervention stress levels, aligning with the challenge-skill balance theory. Qualitative analysis identified core themes such as "digital telepresence" and "liberation from the inner critic," elucidating how a virtual space transforms into a "safe canvas" for emotional catharsis. The results indicate that online intuitive painting serves as a high-potential, flow-based therapeutic strategy for stress management in modern, high-pressure societies, bridging the gap in tele-art therapy literature.

records.title: Advancing microelectronics education: the pedagogical framework of the fames european FD-SOI design school
records.abstract: The rapid advancement of Nanoelectronic technologies is creating new challenges for engineering education, requiring approaches that combine solid theoretical knowledge with practical, hands-on design experience. To address this need, the first edition of the FAMES European FD-SOI Design School (EFDS) was held in Grenoble, France, from January 25-30, 2026. The main objective of this design school was to provide an immersive learning environment to equip participants with advanced knowledge and practical skills in Fully Depleted Silicon on Insulator (FD-SOI) design. This one-week advanced intensive program brought together PhD students, engineers, and researchers from different European institutions. EFDS2026 was developed to help the participants understand how to use FD-SOI to develop more efficient and innovative semiconductor solutions. Participants had the opportunity to explore the full FD-SOI design flow, from transistor modeling and characterization to digital and analog/RF circuit design, including presentations on embedded non-volatile memories in advanced FD-SOI nodes and a session on the design kit. Beyond technical knowledge transfer, a central objective was the development of a structured and transferable design methodology applicable in both academic and industrial contexts. Interactive sessions, collaborative activities, and open technical discussions fostered peer learning and interdisciplinary exchange. Structured surveys revealed highly positive participant feedback. The strong balance between theoretical foundations and hands-on practice, access to advanced design tools, and direct interaction with experts in FD-SOI technology were particularly valued. Participants reported increased confidence in managing complete design flows and expressed strong interest in extended or more advanced training modules. In light of these outcomes, EFDS has been established as an annual initiative, with future editions planned. The long-term objective is the establishment of a sustainable European training platform that strengthens collaboration across academia and research institutions and contributes to the development of highly skilled microelectronics designers. This contribution presents the pedagogical design and instructional strategy of EFDS2026, analyzes participant feedback, and discusses key lessons learned for replicating intensive, technology-focused design schools in advanced engineering domains.

records.title: The Role of Organizational Communication in Building Trust for Delegation: A Georgian Perspective
records.abstract: Annotation. Delegation is one of the most essential functions of management, primarily aimed at enhancing work efficiency and optimizing organizational performance. Beyond task allocation, delegation fosters employees’ professional growth, skill development, and increased motivation by empowering them with responsibilities and autonomy. A strong organizational communication culture plays a pivotal role in the delegation process by facilitating clear expectations, providing ongoing support, and encouraging feedback. In today’s dynamic business environment, where companies are continuously expanding and augmenting their human resources, effective task delegation has become increasingly important to manage growing workloads and complex operations. The success of delegation largely depends on the level of trust established between managers and employees, which is significantly influenced by the quality and transparency of organizational communication. This study focuses on examining the role of organizational communication in building and sustaining trust for delegation within the context of Georgian business organizations. Key factors such as selecting the right personnel, assigning appropriate tasks, setting realistic and clear expectations, granting trust and autonomy to subordinates, and maintaining continuous encouragement and constructive feedback are explored as essential elements of successful delegation. Employing a quantitative research approach, the study utilizes a structured questionnaire survey conducted among managers and non-managers from various Georgian companies. The findings indicate that transparent, consistent, and two-way communication practices substantially strengthen trust, thereby enabling more effective delegation. Furthermore, the research highlights several cultural and contextual factors unique to Georgia that influence communication behaviors and trust-building mechanisms within organizations. The article concludes with practical recommendations aimed at improving organizational communication and reinforcing trust, ultimately contributing to enhanced delegation practices, increased employee satisfaction, and improved overall organizational performance. Keywords: Organizational Communication; Delegation; Trust Building; Management; 1. Introduction In today\`s dynamic and complex business environment, organizations constantly strive for efficiency, adaptability, and competitive advantage. One of the key managerial practices that contribute to achieving these goals is delegation — the process of assigning responsibility and authority to subordinates to carry out specific activities. However, successful delegation does not occur in isolation; it depends on various organizational factors, among which communication and trust play a central role. Effective delegation stems from effective leadership, which empowers employees, motivates them, and fosters accountability throughout the organizational hierarchy. Leaders who delegate appropriately free themselves to concentrate on strategic priorities while simultaneously building competence and leadership potential within their teams. Delegation is considered a vital managerial function that contributes significantly to employee performance and overall organizational success. Effective delegation begins with effective leadership, which serves as the foundation for empowering employees, motivating them, and ensuring accountability. Leaders and managers cannot handle every task on their own, making delegation essential for distributing responsibilities and empowering team members to contribute meaningfully. Delegation is not simply a transfer of tasks, but a strategic process aimed at building trust, developing skills, and improving communication within the organization. When properly implemented, it allows managers to focus on more strategic objectives while simultaneously cultivating leadership capacity among team members. (Ugoani, 2020) Organizational communication is a fundamental component of any institution, as it enables the coordination of activities, the sharing of information, and the building of relationships that drive performance. (Keyton, 2011) defines organizational communication as "the interaction required to direct a group toward a shared goal." In both formal and informal forms, organizational communication fosters understanding, reduces uncertainty, and supports decision-making processes. Within the context of delegation, effective communication ensures clarity of roles, the transmission of expectations, and the creation of feedback loops necessary for performance improvement and employee development. Inadequate communication, on the other hand, can lead to misunderstandings, and poor execution of tasks. Organizational trust comprises employees’ belief in their coworkers’ integrity and competence, as well as confidence in the institution’s supportiveness and fairness. It reflects the extent to which individuals feel secure, respected, and valued within their work environment. (Tichtich & Amira, 2024). Trust not only reduces fear and uncertainty but also enhances performance by encouraging initiative, risk-taking, and feedback-seeking behaviors. Within the delegation process, trust plays a central role—managers must trust employees to fulfill tasks responsibly, while employees must trust that delegated responsibilities are fair and meaningful. Thus, trust acts as a crucial bridge between leadership, communication, and performance in modern organizations. The purpose of this study is to explore the role of organizational communication in fostering trust that supports effective delegation, specifically within Georgian business organizations. This research aims to provide insights into how communication dynamics can be enhanced to strengthen delegation outcomes. The findings are expected to contribute to both theoretical discussions on organizational behavior and practical recommendations for improving communication and trust in the workplace. 1.1 Problem Statement Effective delegation is a critical component of organizational management, yet many organizations face challenges in ensuring that tasks are assigned clearly and executed efficiently. Research indicates that communication quality within an organization significantly influences employees’ trust in leadership and the success of delegated tasks. In the context of Georgian organizations, there is limited empirical evidence exploring how organizational communication shapes trust and impacts delegation effectiveness, highlighting a gap that this study seeks to address. 1.2 Research Objectives To examine the quality and characteristics of organizational communication in selected Georgian companies. To assess the level of trust employees have in their managers and how it relates to delegated tasks. To identify key factors in communication that facilitate effective delegation and reduce misunderstandings or ambiguities. To provide practical recommendations for enhancing organizational communication and trust to improve delegation processes. 1.3 Research Questions How do organizational communication practices influence trust between managers and employees in Georgian organizations? What is the relationship between trust in leadership and the effectiveness of task delegation? How do differences in communication perception between managerial and non-managerial staff affect delegation outcomes? How can improved communication strategies enhance mutual trust and delegation success in Georgian organizations? 2. records.title: From challenge-skills balance to wellbeing in sports: the role of team identification and flow
records.abstract: This study investigated the psychological mechanisms linking challenge-skills balance to psychological wellbeing among team-sport athletes, considering team identification and flow experience as the fundamental drivers of this relationship. A sample of 281 team-sport athletes completed an online survey comprising measures of challenge-skill balance, team identification, flow, and wellbeing. Results supported the hypothesized model: Athletes who perceived their competencies as congruent with competitive demands reported stronger team identification, which in turn was related to deeper flow experiences. Flow was then associated with wellbeing, mediating the effect of team identification. These findings highlight the interconnected role of cognitive resources, social identity processes, and optimal experiential states in sustaining athletes' psychological wellbeing.
